alt: A comparison of malaria and cholera. Malaria is caused by the Plasmodium parasite, reaches people through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, and is linked to water because larvae develop in still water. Cholera is caused by a bacterium, spreads through water or food contaminated with faeces, and is linked to untreated sewage.
caption: Malaria travels by mosquito; cholera travels in water contaminated with faeces.

alt: A cycle. 1: the vector is the female Anopheles mosquito, which needs blood to make eggs. 2: an infected mosquito passes the Plasmodium parasite to a human when it bites. 3: a non-infected mosquito picks up the parasite when it feeds on an infected human; the parasite develops inside it. Females lay eggs on still water, where larvae live.
caption: Human to mosquito and mosquito to human: the cycle needs people, mosquitoes and the parasite.

alt: Malaria strategies grouped by the link they break. Stop the bite: insecticide-treated bed nets and repellent. Fewer mosquitoes: cover or drain breeding areas, spray insecticides, release sterilised males, biological control such as larva-eating fish. Less infection in people: vaccination of young children and antimalarial drugs.
caption: Stop the bite, cut the mosquito numbers, or cut infection in people.

alt: Cholera passes from an infected person’s faeces into water or food and then into another person. Barrier A keeps faeces out of water through handwashing and sanitation with sewage treatment. Barrier B makes water safe by boiling or chlorination. C protects the person with oral cholera vaccine. Cholera has no vector.
caption: Keep faeces out of water, make water safe, or vaccinate the person.

alt: A benefit and a limitation for each malaria strategy. Treated nets are cheap but only protect in bed at night and face resistance. Repellent must be reapplied. Vaccination gives partial protection. Drugs face cost and resistance. Draining breeding sites is impossible over huge wetlands. Spraying harms pollinators. Sterile males are expensive and slow. Biological control may harm native species.
caption: Every malaria strategy has a catch: resistance, cost, scale or harm to other species.

alt: A benefit and a limitation for each cholera strategy. Handwashing is very cheap but needs soap, water and behaviour change. Sanitation and sewage treatment remove the cause permanently but cost a lot and take time. Boiling kills bacteria but needs fuel. Chlorination treats large volumes but needs chemicals and staff. Vaccination protects quickly but is not lifelong and does not fix the water supply.
caption: Sanitation fixes the cause but is slow and costly; quicker measures do not fix the water supply.
